strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: graph contrastive learning augmentations are often biologically implausible for gene regulatory networks, and using real knockdown data as supervision is a promising direction.

The proposed framework is clearly motivated and connects node-level contrastive learning with augmentation-level similarity between artificial and biological perturbations. The decomposition in Theorem 1 gives a useful conceptual lens for thinking about supervised augmentation selection.

The empirical setting is nontrivial, spanning TCGA/LINCS-derived GRNs for breast, lung, and colorectal cancers, with both node-level and graph-level downstream tasks. The appendices provide useful details on datasets, GRN construction, hyperparameters, and compute.
The paper reports multiple metrics in the appendix and includes comparisons against several graph representation learning baselines using a shared Graph Transformer backbone.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is overstated. SupGCL is often only marginally better than baselines, with standard deviations overlapping in many main-table results, e.g. hazard prediction and several node-level tasks. The manuscript itself notes that superiority is not statistically significant in every task, but still claims consistent outperformance and significantly higher performance without reporting statistical tests.

Theoretical soundness is not fully convincing. The augmentation reference distribution p_phi(b|a) is computed using the same trainable GNN as q_phi, so the stated trivial-solution concern remains unless a stop-gradient, teacher freezing, or other asymmetry is specified. The theorem assumes a factorization of p_phi but does not justify why the learned model satisfies it or how this prevents collapse in the actual algorithm.

Algorithmic details appear inconsistent with the objective. In Algorithm 1, the node-level loss is written as an average of log q_phi(i|i,a,b), whereas minimizing the KL/cross-entropy form should involve a negative log-likelihood. This sign error, together with the informal importance-sampling treatment, makes the implemented optimization unclear.

The evaluation lacks several important controls. There is no ablation separating the augmentation-level loss, supervised sampling distribution, artificial knockdown masking, and teacher GRNs. It is therefore hard to know which component drives the gains. There is also no comparison to simpler biologically informed augmentations or supervised/pretraining baselines outside generic GCL methods.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper says the implementation and experimental code are available, but the URL is blank. Reproducing the GRN estimation also requires substantial Fugaku compute, specialized INGOR/SiGN-BN processing, and many preprocessing choices that may be difficult to reconstruct exactly.

The downstream task design raises concerns. Node-level GO/OncoKB labels are fixed gene annotations, while embeddings are learned from repeated patient graphs over the same 975 genes; gene-wise cross-validation may not test generalization to new biological settings. The biological interpretation of modest accuracy gains on these labels is not deeply analyzed.

Presentation is generally understandable, but some notation is confusing: p_phi is called a reference distribution while being parameterized by the trainable model, the relationship between patient GRNs and multiple teacher GRNs is underspecified in the main method, and some figures/tables are too small or qualitative to substantiate the claims.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The limitation only notes same-cancer teacher GRNs, but does not discuss cell-line-to-patient domain shift, biases in TCGA/LINCS/GO/OncoKB annotations, uncertainty in inferred GRNs, or risks of interpreting the model for clinical/therapeutic conclusions.

strengths: The core idea is relevant and potentially useful: replacing arbitrary graph augmentations with biologically grounded perturbations from gene knockdown experiments is a sensible direction for GRN representation learning.

The paper evaluates on multiple downstream tasks across three cancer types, including node-level functional labels and graph-level survival/subtype tasks, which is broader than a single-task benchmark.
The manuscript provides some useful dataset and preprocessing detail in the appendices, including TCGA/LINCS sources, GRN estimation settings, label construction, and compute times.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence does not support the strength of the claims. Most reported gains over the best baseline are small relative to the reported standard deviations, and the paper provides no statistical tests. The claim that SupGCL achieves significantly higher or consistently superior performance is therefore unsupported.

Additional metrics in the appendix weaken the main conclusion: SupGCL is not best on several Macro F1 and Jaccard results, contradicting the abstract/introduction claim that it outperforms baselines across all experiments.

The method’s theoretical justification is underdeveloped. The reference distribution is produced by the same trainable GNN as the target distribution, so the teacher signal is not fixed; the paper does not convincingly rule out degenerate or arbitrary alignment. The theorem is mostly a KL decomposition under assumptions whose connection to the implemented algorithm is unclear.

There appears to be a serious sign error in Algorithm 1: the node contrastive loss is written as an average of log q(i|i,a,b), whereas the KL/InfoNCE form should minimize negative log probability. This raises concerns about implementation correctness and reproducibility.

The evaluation lacks essential ablations: no comparison to random teacher GRNs, artificial knockdown masking without teacher supervision, shuffled knockdown labels, cross-cancer teachers, or variants separating the augmentation-level loss from the node-level loss. As a result, it is unclear whether gains come from the proposed biological supervision or incidental training differences.

Baselines are limited and not fully convincing for the biological setting. The paper compares generic graph SSL methods but does not include strong domain-specific GRN representation baselines or simple supervised baselines using expression/edge features directly.

Reproducibility is poor. The code availability statement is incomplete, and key details are missing: exact architecture parameters, Optuna trial counts and selection protocol, random seeds, train/validation/test split construction, early stopping criteria, and implementation details for sampling the softmax normalizers.

The GRN construction pipeline is computationally heavy and depends on specialized supercomputer resources, but the paper does not provide released processed GRNs or a practical reproduction path. This materially limits independent verification.

Presentation has several issues: the paper overinterprets t-SNE plots, relies heavily on subset accuracy for imbalanced multi-label tasks, contains typos and formatting problems, and makes stronger claims than the tables justify.

The limitations and ethics discussion are minimal. The paper uses public biomedical datasets, but it does not discuss privacy, clinical validity, possible misuse in biomedical interpretation, or the risk of overclaiming patient-level predictive utility from modest retrospective benchmarks.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: standard GCL augmentations are often biologically implausible for gene regulatory networks, and using real knockdown perturbations as supervision is a natural and potentially useful direction.

The proposed SupGCL objective is conceptually appealing. It connects node-level contrastive learning with an augmentation-level distribution induced by teacher GRNs, and the formulation gives a clean view of conventional GCL as a limiting case when the augmentation temperature is large.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this application area: three cancer types, patient-level and gene-level downstream tasks, multiple GCL/graph representation baselines, and additional metrics and embedding-dimension analyses in the appendix.

Results are consistently favorable to SupGCL in the main reported metrics, especially for graph-level hazard prediction and breast cancer subtype classification, and the latent-space visualizations are directionally consistent with the quantitative findings.
The appendices provide useful dataset, GRN-estimation, hyperparameter, and computation-time details, which helps assess the experimental setup.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are often small relative to the reported standard deviations, and the paper explicitly notes that SupGCL is not statistically superior on every task. The abstract and contribution statements overclaim by saying SupGCL outperforms baselines across all experiments without adequately qualifying statistical uncertainty.

The strongest comparison is somewhat confounded because SupGCL uses additional LINCS knockdown supervision while most baselines do not. The paper would be more convincing with ablations isolating the value of teacher GRNs, augmentation-level loss, node-level loss, temperature choices, and a supervised non-contrastive pretraining alternative using the same extra data.

There is a potential transductive evaluation concern: pretraining appears to use patient-specific GRNs before downstream 10-fold evaluation, but it is not clear whether test-fold patient graphs are excluded from pretraining. If all patient graphs are used in self-supervised pretraining, the graph-level downstream results may not reflect a fully inductive setting.

The theoretical contribution is limited. Theorem 1 is mainly a KL-chain-rule decomposition under an independence assumption; it does not by itself establish avoidance of collapse or biological faithfulness. Since both teacher and target distributions are parameterized by the same trainable GNN, the role of the reference distribution and whether gradients are stopped through p_phi should be clarified.

Algorithm 1 appears to contain a sign error in the node-level loss: it defines Lossa,b_node as the average log q_phi(i|i,a,b), whereas minimizing the loss should use negative log likelihood or KL-equivalent cross entropy. This is likely a typo but is important for reproducibility.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript states that implementation and experimental code are available, but the link appears missing. The GRN estimation pipeline also requires large-scale computation on Fugaku, and more explicit scripts, checkpoints, processed networks, and split definitions would be needed for reliable reproduction.

The biological scope is narrower than some claims suggest: teacher GRNs are constructed from cancer cell lines matched to cancer type, while downstream patient GRNs come from TCGA. This cross-domain teacher-student setup is plausible but not deeply validated biologically, and the limitation discussion is quite brief.

Ethics and data governance are not discussed in much detail. The datasets are public, but the work uses human cancer patient data, so a short statement on privacy, consent provenance, and intended biomedical use would be appropriate.

strengths: The paper proposes a meaningful and biologically motivated direction: using real knockdown-derived perturbation information to supervise graph contrastive learning for gene regulatory networks, rather than relying only on artificial graph augmentations or avoiding augmentations entirely.

The probabilistic formulation is clear at a high level and usefully connects supervised augmentation weighting with conventional node-level GCL as a limiting case when the augmentation temperature becomes large.

The empirical section is broad for a specialized bio-ML paper: three cancer types, node-level gene function/cancer relevance tasks, graph-level survival/subtype tasks, additional metrics, link prediction, cross-domain tests, robustness analyses, and enrichment analysis.
The appendices provide many practical details on TCGA/LINCS preprocessing, Bayesian-network GRN construction, hyperparameter search, compute cost, and downstream training settings.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not fully supported statistically. The main tables show SupGCL is often best, but improvements are usually small relative to the reported standard deviations, and the authors state that most Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons are not significant. This weakens the claim of consistent superiority across 13 tasks.

There is a potential evaluation-design concern: pretraining appears to use all patient-specific TCGA GRNs before 10-fold downstream cross-validation. For graph-level patient prediction, this makes the evaluation transductive and may expose the representation learner to test-patient gene-expression graphs, which should be clearly separated or reported as a distinct setting.

The biological supervision is less direct than the framing suggests. Teacher GRNs are inferred from LINCS cancer cell-line shRNA experiments, not directly observed regulatory networks in patients, and artificial knockdown is modeled by zeroing one gene and incident edge features. The paper does not sufficiently validate that this augmentation/teacher pairing faithfully captures biological perturbation effects.

The method section has technical ambiguities. Both augmentation-level teacher and target distributions are parameterized by the same GNN, and the treatment of gradients through the teacher distribution is not clearly specified. Algorithm 1 also appears to define the node contrastive loss with a positive log q term rather than the expected negative log-likelihood/KL contribution, making implementation details hard to trust.

Baseline coverage is reasonable but not fully convincing for the biological setting. Some stronger domain-specific or supervised alternatives for survival/subtype prediction and GRN representation learning are missing, and some added baselines are evaluated only on breast cancer and only two tasks.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release or exact executable pipeline is indicated, and reproducing the GRN construction requires substantial external data processing and supercomputer-scale Bayesian-network estimation. Random seeds and Optuna trial budgets are also not fully specified.

The limitations discussion is honest but narrow. It mentions poor direct cross-cancer transfer, but does not adequately discuss transductive evaluation, inferred-GRN uncertainty, cell-line-to-patient mismatch, possible shRNA off-target effects, or ethical/privacy considerations around clinical survival data, even though public TCGA data reduces the direct human-subject risk.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: using real perturbation data for GRN representation learning is a sensible and potentially useful direction, especially compared with purely artificial graph augmentations.

The manuscript provides a reasonably broad empirical surface, including node-level biological annotation tasks, graph-level survival/subtype prediction, link prediction, cross-domain tests, robustness checks, and biological enrichment analyses.

The appendix contains useful implementation details about GRN construction, datasets, hyperparameter ranges, compute time, and additional metrics, which improves transparency relative to many submissions.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is not convincingly supported. The reported gains over baselines are generally small relative to standard deviations, and the appendix states that most pairwise comparisons are not statistically significant. The paper nevertheless repeatedly claims consistent superiority and significantly higher performance, which overstates the evidence.

There appears to be a serious evaluation-design concern: pretraining is described as using patient-specific TCGA GRNs before downstream 10-fold cross-validation. If the pretrained encoder sees all patient graphs, including those later used as test folds, the setting is transductive and may leak test-sample expression/network information into representation learning. This is especially problematic for graph-level survival and subtype prediction.

The theoretical formulation is weak. Both teacher and learned distributions are parameterized by the same GNN, making collapse an acknowledged risk, but the proposed resolution is not rigorously justified. Theorem 1 mainly decomposes KL under strong independence assumptions rather than proving that the method learns biologically meaningful representations. The algorithm also contains apparent sign/definition issues, e.g. the node loss is written as an average of log q rather than negative log q/KL, making the actual optimized objective unclear.

The biological supervision is less direct than claimed. The “teacher GRNs” are themselves estimated from LINCS cell-line knockdown expression data using a Bayesian-network pipeline, not experimentally observed regulatory graphs. Thus the method depends heavily on noisy inferred GRNs and cross-domain assumptions between cell lines and TCGA patients, but the paper does not validate whether these teacher networks are biologically faithful.

Baselines and ablations are insufficient for the claims. The method is compared mainly to generic graph SSL methods; there is no strong supervised or semi-supervised biological pretraining baseline that uses the same knockdown data in a simpler way, no ablation separating the augmentation-level loss from the supervised sampling term, and limited analysis of whether improvements come from extra data, extra computation, or the proposed contrastive formulation.

Several downstream tasks are weak proxies for biological usefulness. GO/OncoKB labels are coarse and partly generic, subset accuracies are low, cancer-relevance classification uses undersampling and accuracy despite severe imbalance, and survival improvements are modest. The enrichment analysis is qualitative and post hoc, with limited controls for cluster size, multiple testing, or baseline enrichment strength.

Reproducibility remains limited despite detailed appendices. The paper does not appear to provide code, processed datasets, exact Optuna trial budgets/seeds, fold definitions, or enough detail to recreate the GRN estimation pipeline without substantial specialized infrastructure such as Fugaku and large LINCS preprocessing.

The limitations and ethics discussion are too narrow. The paper mentions cross-cancer generalization failure, but does not adequately discuss patient-data leakage risks, clinical misuse of survival/subtype predictions, uncertainty in inferred GRNs, or the limitations of transferring cell-line perturbation data to patient tumors.

strengths: The paper proposes a compelling and domain-motivated idea: using real gene knockdown perturbation data as supervised augmentation information for graph contrastive learning on GRNs. This is more biologically grounded than random edge/node perturbations and is a meaningful conceptual contribution.
The method is presented in a unified probabilistic GCL framework, with a clear connection to conventional node-level GCL as a limiting case when the augmentation-temperature parameter becomes large.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this domain: three cancer types, node-level tasks, graph-level patient tasks, cross-domain experiments, robustness checks, embedding-dimension analysis, link prediction, and biological enrichment analysis.

SupGCL consistently performs best or near-best in the main downstream tables, including hazard prediction, subtype prediction, BP/CC classification, and cancer-related gene classification. The gains are especially encouraging because the same Graph Transformer backbone is used across methods.

The appendices provide useful dataset, preprocessing, hyperparameter, compute-time, and GRN-estimation details, and the authors honestly discuss a real limitation: poor robustness when a fine-tuned model is directly applied out of cancer type.
weaknesses: The statistical evidence is weaker than the headline claims suggest. The paper acknowledges that most Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons are not significant, with significance only against GraphCL/SGRL on a few node-level tasks. Many main-table improvements are small relative to standard deviations, so the claim of consistent superiority should be softened.

The central optimization is not fully soundly specified. The teacher distribution p_phi is parameterized by the same GNN as q_phi, and it is unclear whether gradients are stopped through p_phi or whether any fixed teacher/reference mechanism is used. This matters because the manuscript itself notes collapse risks when both distributions are optimized, and the node-level loss may not fully justify the supervised interpretation.

There is a possible sign or implementation ambiguity in the pseudocode: the node-level loss is written as an average of log q rather than negative log q / KL with a delta target. This could be a typo, but it weakens reproducibility for a method paper.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives many implementation details, but I did not see a code release, exact Optuna trial budgets, full baseline implementation details, or enough information to reproduce the expensive GRN construction pipeline without substantial specialized infrastructure such as Fugaku/INGOR.

The evaluation could better isolate where gains come from. Since SupGCL uses additional LINCS knockdown supervision unavailable to ordinary self-supervised baselines, stronger ablations are needed to separate the value of extra biological data from the value of the proposed probabilistic formulation.

Some downstream tasks are relatively coarse or potentially easy to exploit from shared gene identities, especially node-level GO/OncoKB labels over the same 975 genes. The gene-wise cross-validation protocol should more clearly justify that it tests representation quality rather than memorization of gene-specific annotation structure.

Ethics and limitations are underdeveloped for biomedical prediction. The paper uses public cancer datasets and does not deploy clinical decisions, but it should discuss patient-data provenance, possible demographic/cohort biases, and the risks of interpreting survival or subtype predictions as clinically actionable.
